summary: People sharing one language build a city and tower in Shinar to make a name and avoid dispersal, but Yahweh confuses their speech and scatters them. A genealogy then follows Shem to Terah, whose family includes Abram, Sarai, and Lot and travels from Ur toward Canaan as far as Haran.
whyItMatters: The chapter moves from the many nations of chapter 10 to the particular family addressed by God in chapter 12. Sarai’s childlessness and the family’s unfinished journey make the coming promises more pointed.

context.author: Genesis names no historical writer. Jewish and Christian tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the book briefing describes older traditions shaped into a final literary form, without a settled account of every stage.
context.audience: The book addresses Israel through a story of shared human origins and the family from whom Israel traces its ancestry; no single first audience is named in this chapter.
context.date: The narrated events belong to primeval or ancestral time, not to a securely dated writing event. Major stages of Genesis are often placed across the monarchic to Persian periods, with exact models and dates debated.
context.setting: The plain of Shinar and later family locations at Ur of the Chaldees and Haran.
context.literaryForm: Babel story followed by a lineage from Shem and a family travel notice.

before.text: Chapter 10 maps Noah’s descendants into families, languages, lands, and nations. Chapter 11 first tells a dispersal story, then narrows one ancestral line.

here.text: Watch the turn at verse 10: the account leaves Babel for Shem’s descendants and finally Terah’s household, including Sarai’s childlessness.

after.text: Yahweh calls Abram to leave his country and promises land, descendants, and blessing for all families of the earth.

outline.heading: One language and a city plan
outline.note: The builders seek a lasting name and fear being scattered.

outline.heading: Speech confused and builders scattered
outline.note: Yahweh comes down, changes mutual understanding, and the city is left unfinished.

outline.heading: Shem’s line to Terah
outline.note: The genealogy follows named generations from after the flood to Abram’s father.

outline.heading: Terah’s family and interrupted journey
outline.note: Haran dies, marriages are named, Sarai has no child, and the travelers stop in Haran.

keyVerses.text: They said, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth.”
keyVerses.why: The builders’ own words state their aim and fear of dispersal.

keyVerses.text: Therefore its name was called Babel, because there Yahweh confused the language of all the earth. From there, Yahweh scattered them abroad on the surface of all the earth.
keyVerses.why: The verse names Babel and links the place with confused language and scattering.

keyVerses.text: Sarai was barren. She had no child.
keyVerses.why: Sarai’s childlessness introduces a serious tension before the promise of a great nation.

questions.question: Why do the builders make a tower?
questions.answer: They plan a city and tower to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered across the earth. The passage states their fear and ambition, not a need to shelter from a second flood.

questions.question: Why is the city called Babel here?
questions.answer: The narrator links its name to Yahweh’s confusing the builders’ shared language there. The story itself explains the name through that action and repeats that the people were scattered from the place.

questions.question: Is speaking one language presented as evil in itself?
questions.answer: The text begins with common speech and then reports a collective city project meant to resist dispersal. God’s response addresses what the people have begun to do together; it does not state that every shared language or cooperation is wrong.

questions.question: How does this story relate to the languages already listed in chapter 10?
questions.answer: The preceding table describes peoples as they have spread into languages and lands, while this chapter narrates a language-and-scattering episode. Genesis places these accounts together without requiring readers to treat every paragraph as one continuous clock sequence.

questions.question: Why does Yahweh confuse speech rather than simply tell them to stop?
questions.answer: The account has Yahweh say they are one people and will not be restrained from their intended action, then change their ability to understand one another. It reports the result but does not give a full moral analysis of every builder.

questions.question: What is the “history of the generations of Shem”?
questions.answer: It is a lineage heading after the Babel story, tracing births through successive fathers toward Terah. The repeated notice of more sons and daughters shows that the list selects one route through a wider family.

questions.question: Where does Terah’s family intend to go, and where does it stop?
questions.answer: Terah takes Abram, Sarai, and Lot from Ur of the Chaldees with Canaan as the stated destination. They come to Haran and live there; Abram’s onward departure belongs to the next chapter.

questions.question: Why mention that Sarai has no child just before God promises Abram a nation?
questions.answer: The chapter gives no explanation for her barrenness, but its placement makes the promised descendants an apparent impossibility. The notice should not be turned into a judgment on Sarai or on people unable to have children.

questions.question: Why does the hosted Brenton edition name Cainan where WEB names Shelah?
questions.answer: WEB 11:12 says Arpachshad fathered Shelah, while the hosted Brenton edition says Arphaxad fathered Cainan and then places Sala in the following generation. These English versions follow different textual traditions; comparing them does not establish which ancient reading is earliest.

glossary.def: The land containing the plain where the city and tower project begins.
The city named at the scene of confused speech and dispersal.
The chapter’s description of Sarai having no child, without stating a moral cause.
